**Merge** keeps the full history of both branches, then joins them with a merge commit. It's safe — your work stays exactly as it was.

**Rebase** rewrites your branch's history by replaying your commits on top of the new base. It's cleaner — you get a straight line instead of branching paths.

When to merge: You want to preserve what happened and when. Good for long-running branches where the history itself matters (release branches, important feature work). Safe when collaborating because you never rewrite.

When to rebase: Before you merge to main, to clean up a messy branch. Makes the main line readable and makes `git log` tell a story. Also good for keeping your local branch up to date without cluttering the history.

**The catch:** Never rebase commits that other people have pulled. Rewriting history that's already shared breaks their copy. Use it only on branches you own.

**The pattern most teams use:** Rebase locally while you're working to keep things tidy. Merge to main with a merge commit (or squash-merge for small fixes) so main's history is clear. Then main stays clean and shared, and your workspace is nimble.

If your repo has a CLAUDE.md file, check it — your team might have a rule about which to use where.
